title: ASME Audit Support in Houston | NDE Level III Prep
description: ASME joint review prep for Houston vessel and exchanger shops: NDE written practice, Section V procedures, subcontractor control, mock review. Ask us.
h1: ASME Certification Audit Support in Houston: NDE Readiness for Gulf Coast Stamp Shops
html:
This page is for quality managers and NDE coordinators at Houston-area pressure vessel, heat exchanger and process skid fabricators that hold, or are applying for, an ASME Certificate of Authorization. Atlantis NDT has an office in Houston, and an ASNT NDT Level III from Atlantis prepares the nondestructive examination side of your quality control system for the joint review: the written practice, the Section V procedures, NDE subcontractor control and the records the review team will pull. Tell us when your review is due and we will scope the work with you.

Who builds and repairs pressure equipment around Houston

Houston carries a heavy concentration of Code fabrication because the refineries, chemical plants, LNG terminals and gas processors it serves buy pressure equipment constantly. Shops along the Ship Channel corridor and around the Beltway build Section VIII Division 1 vessels, shell-and-tube exchangers, separators, filter housings, knockout drums and complete process skids. A smaller group holds Division 2 certificates for heavy-wall reactors and high-pressure service. Module yards assemble packaged plant sections for export. Boiler manufacturing is a smaller slice of the local market, but package boilers, waste heat components and boiler external piping keep some S, A and PP certificate holders busy, and National Board R certificate holders work inside plants during turnarounds.

What these shops share is volume and schedule pressure. A busy vessel shop can have dozens of Code jobs open at once, each with its own radiography map, purchaser-added examinations, positive material identification and data report. The joint review samples that workload. The team wants to see that the NDE controls described in your quality control manual are what actually happens to a real job on your floor, not a description of a tidier shop you would like to be.

How the joint review runs in Texas

In Texas the state takes part directly. The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR) supplies the team leader for joint reviews of manufacturers and repair organizations, and the team also includes the Authorized Inspector Supervisor and the Authorized Inspector from your Authorized Inspection Agency. TDLR describes a two-day review: the quality control system on day one, then implementation on a demonstration item on day two. Its recommendation goes to ASME or the National Board, which make the decision on the certificate.

Joint reviews are required for a new Certificate of Authorization and again every three years for renewal. TDLR asks the AIA of record to send the scheduling request, and it books a review roughly two and a half months out once the readiness items are in. Its guidance is to start three to six months ahead for a new certificate and about six months before expiration for a renewal. That lead time is the window in which NDE gaps should be found and closed, rather than the week before the team arrives.

Two features of the TDLR process matter for NDE. The manual review normally happens off site and in private, with no applicant staff in the room, so the NDE sections of your manual must make sense to a reader who cannot ask you what you meant. And during implementation the team interviews the people who hold quality duties. If your NDE coordinator, or whoever reviews subcontractor radiographs, cannot walk the team through what they check and why, that becomes obvious in minutes.

The Texas jurisdiction, and the ones your equipment ships to

Texas regulates boilers under Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code, administered by the TDLR Boiler Program under its Chief Boiler Inspector. Boilers in Texas carry a state number, need a certificate of operation, and are inspected by commissioned inspectors employed by an Authorized Inspection Agency or by TDLR deputy inspectors. The Texas statute is written around boilers. For unfired vessels built in Houston, the jurisdictional demands usually reach the shop through the place where the vessel will be installed and through the purchaser's specification, which commonly requires National Board registration of the Manufacturer's Data Report.

That matters because Houston fabricators ship everywhere: into neighboring states with their own pressure vessel programs, into Canadian provinces that require a Canadian Registration Number for the design, and overseas. Your quality control manual has to cover the NDE that the construction Code edition requires, and each job file has to show any extra examination that a jurisdiction or purchaser added. Expect a team member to pick a job that shipped out of state and ask how its examination requirements reached the traveler and the NDE request.

How Houston stamp shops handle NDE

Most Houston fabricators split their NDE. Visual examination, and often magnetic particle and liquid penetrant, are done by the shop's own Level II personnel certified under the shop's written practice. Radiography is nearly always subcontracted to licensed radiography companies, because radiation licensing, exposure areas and source logistics are a business of their own. Ultrasonic work, including phased array used in place of radiography where Section VIII permits it, is mixed: some shops employ UT technicians, while many bring in a contractor job by job.

That split creates the two places where Houston shops most often collect NDE findings. The in-house program is one: a written practice still citing an outdated edition of SNT-TC-1A, Level II certifications with no documented experience hours, lapsed annual vision examinations, or an MT yoke with no lift-test record. The subcontractor interface is the other: the manual says the shop approves its NDE subcontractors, but the file holds a purchase order and a capability brochure rather than the subcontractor's written practice, procedures and current technician certifications.

Both are easy to fix with time and hard to fix in a week. Our written practice work and the SNT-TC-1A hours planner help with the first; the subcontractor file is covered below.

NDE subcontractor control: what the team expects to find

When a certificate holder subcontracts NDE, it keeps the responsibility for it. The team will look for the part of your manual that says how you evaluate an NDE subcontractor before use, what you require it to submit, how its procedures are accepted for your work, and how the Authorized Inspector reaches its personnel records and examination results. Then the team tests that wording against a real job. For a Houston shop the file usually needs:

  • A current copy of the subcontractor's written practice, reviewed against SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, whichever your Code edition and contract call for.
  • Its procedures for each method it performs on your work, checked against Section V Article 1, the method article and the construction Code, with a record of who accepted them for you.
  • Certifications, vision records and Level III identification for each technician who examined your welds, valid on the date of examination.
  • Radiographs or UT data that your organization reviewed and accepted before the Authorized Inspector saw them, with the review signature traceable to a named, trained person.
  • A way to suspend a subcontractor that fails, and evidence that you have used it or at least considered it.

An Atlantis Level III builds this file with you: reading the subcontractor's written practice and procedures, flagging gaps, and drafting the acceptance record your manual calls for. Since Atlantis shoots no radiographs anywhere in the US, it has no stake in the outcome when it reads a radiography company's procedures and film for you. The broader method for checking any NDE supplier is on our subcontractor approval audits page.

The demonstration item and the NDE on it

An applicant for a new certificate demonstrates its quality control system on an item built for the designator and scope it is requesting: actual Code work, a mock-up, or both. ASME's description of the joint review is blunt that the demonstration must implement every aspect of the system. If your manual says welds are radiographed by a subcontractor under your control, the team expects to watch that happen on the demonstration item, with the procedure, technique, images, interpretation and your review. If your scope includes ultrasonic examination in place of radiography, expect the same scrutiny of the UT procedure, the qualification and the data.

TDLR notes that a welder must be present to weld the demonstration item. Plan the NDE the same way. Book the radiography contractor for that day, confirm that the technician's certification and the procedure revision on site match your file, and have the person who reviews radiographs ready to explain what they accept and why. A beautifully welded mock-up examined by a lab whose paperwork you have never seen tells the team more than you want it to.

Process piping and skids under the stamp program

Many Houston shops build skids where the vessel carries the Certification Mark and the interconnecting piping is built to ASME B31.3. B31.3 has no Certification Mark of its own, yet purchasers often require that piping to run through the same quality control system and the same NDE controls. Shops building boiler external piping to B31.1 under a PP certificate face the question directly in the review. Either way, piping examination rules, random examination percentages and acceptance criteria differ from those of Section VIII. Travelers and NDE request forms need to name the code that governs each weld, because a radiographer reading film against the wrong acceptance table is a finding in waiting. Our pages on ASME B31.3 and ASME B31.1 summarize the piping side.

What Atlantis does for a Houston joint review, and what it does not

Because Atlantis has an office in Houston, most local work combines remote document review with time on your floor. Houston engagements are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, who founded Atlantis; his ASNT NDT Level III covers the UT, RT, MT, PT and VT methods and rests on 11+ years of shop and plant work abroad and at home. For the NDE portion of a joint review we:

  • Review or write the NDE written practice and align it with the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition that your Code edition references.
  • Review NDE procedures and technique sheets against Section V (Article 2 for radiography, Article 4 for ultrasonics, and the MT, PT and VT articles) and the construction Code, and write the ones that are missing through our procedure development service.
  • Prepare and witness procedure demonstrations where Section V or the Code calls for them.
  • Audit personnel files for training, experience, examinations and vision, using the checks described on our training records and vision records pages.
  • Build the NDE subcontractor file and draft NDE wording for the subcontracting and examination sections of your manual, for your quality manager to adopt.
  • Run a mock review of the NDE portion against the team's checklist, then help you close findings with corrective-action evidence.

Some things stay outside our role. Atlantis is not your Authorized Inspection Agency, the Authorized Inspector, ASME or the team leader, and we sign no data reports. The quality control manual belongs to the certificate holder, and the AIA accepts it. The welding program, meaning welding procedure specifications, procedure qualification records and welder qualifications, belongs to you and your welding engineer; Atlantis does not write or qualify welding procedures, and our WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer covers how those documents fit together. Section III nuclear certificates are outside our scope.

Houston readiness checklist for the NDE portion

  1. Confirm the Code edition your manual cites and the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 edition that edition references, then check that your written practice matches.
  2. Pull every in-house NDE certification and check the expiry date, the vision examination date and documented experience by method.
  3. For each radiography and UT subcontractor used since the last review, assemble its written practice, procedures, technician certifications and your acceptance record.
  4. Choose three completed jobs, at least one shipped out of state, and trace the NDE from traveler to request to report to data report.
  5. Check calibration records: UT instruments and calibration blocks, MT yokes and their lift tests, light meters, and the densitometers and step wedges your RT subcontractor uses.
  6. Confirm the manual names the person who reviews radiographs and UT data, and that the training behind that role is documented.
  7. Plan demonstration-day NDE: contractor booked, technician certification on file, procedure revision matched to the job.
  8. Separate purchaser-added tests such as PMI and hardness from Code examinations in your travelers so nobody confuses the two.
  9. Gather the corrective-action evidence for findings from the last review in one place.
  10. Brief the people the team will interview, using plain questions about what they actually do.

If certification expiries and calibration due dates are tracked on spreadsheets, our pages on expired technician certifications and certificate tracking explain how to keep that evidence current between reviews.

How an engagement runs and what to send

Send us the designators you hold or are applying for, the date your AIA expects the review, the manual sections on examination, NDE, subcontracting and records, your written practice, your NDE procedures, and a list of NDE subcontractors used since the last review. We read them remotely and return a gap list keyed to the manual paragraph and the Code requirement behind each item. Then we spend time at your shop checking files and the floor, run a mock review of the NDE portion, and stay available while you close items. For your Level II technicians, our NDT training in Houston follows SNT-TC-1A, while the act of certifying each Level II stays with your company.

For other Gulf Coast work, see our Houston NDT consulting page; for a standing arrangement, see Level III of record in Houston; and for the full scope of this service, see the national ASME audit Level III support page. If you also hold an R certificate, our NBIC R-stamp NDT audit support page covers that review. Neighbors on the Oklahoma side of the supply chain can read our Tulsa ASME audit support notes.

faq.q: How far ahead should a Houston shop start preparing the NDE side of a joint review?
faq.a: TDLR suggests starting three to six months ahead for a new certificate and about six months before expiration for a renewal. NDE gaps such as missing experience records or an outdated written practice take weeks to close properly, so begin the NDE review as soon as the AIA starts scheduling.

faq.q: Who leads an ASME joint review in Texas?
faq.a: TDLR provides the team leader, joined by the Authorized Inspector Supervisor and the Authorized Inspector from your AIA. TDLR makes a recommendation, and ASME or the National Board decide on the certificate.

faq.q: Our radiography is subcontracted. What records does the team expect from us?
faq.a: The subcontractor's written practice, its procedures accepted for your work, technician certifications and vision records valid on the examination dates, and evidence that someone in your organization reviewed the radiographs before the Authorized Inspector. Our subcontractor approval audit page explains how to build that file.

faq.q: Do we need our own Level III to hold an ASME certificate?
faq.a: Your written practice needs a Level III behind it for the methods you use, but that person does not have to be an employee. Many Houston shops use an outside Level III under a documented arrangement; see Level III of record in Houston.

faq.q: Can Atlantis be our radiography subcontractor?
faq.a: No. Radiographic exposures are not part of what Atlantis does in this country. We can review your radiography company's procedures and images as a Level III, and we can perform UT, MT, PT and VT at your site; see inspection services in Houston.

faq.q: Can you help us use phased array instead of radiography on Section VIII welds?
faq.a: Yes, on the NDE side. We review or write the UT procedure to Section V Article 4 and the construction Code's conditions, plan the qualification or demonstration the Code requires, and check the data review process. Whether the substitution suits a given vessel is your engineering and purchaser decision.

faq.q: Will someone from Atlantis be at the joint review?
faq.a: We can be on site in Houston if you want support during implementation, but the team decides who sits in which session, and the manual review is usually done privately. Most of our value is in the months before the visit.

faq.q: Do you write our quality control manual?
faq.a: We draft the NDE wording for the examination and subcontracting sections, and your quality manager adopts it. The manual is the certificate holder's document, and your AIA accepts it.

faq.q: Do you support Section III nuclear certificates?
faq.a: No. Nuclear certificates under Section III are outside our scope. We work on the NDE portion of non-nuclear certificate reviews.

faq.q: Can you train our technicians for the certifications the team will check?
faq.a: Our Houston NDT training and Level 2 courses follow SNT-TC-1A. A course prepares people; the certificate on file still comes from your own employer program.
